task.effect_definition: mean rating of version A minus mean rating of version B, in scale points

factors.name: Intention vs. accident
factors.description: Whether a person brings about an outcome on purpose or by accident; the physical act and the outcome are held fixed.

factors.name: Doing vs. allowing
factors.description: Whether a person actively brings about an outcome or merely allows it when they could have prevented it; outcome, knowledge, motive and ease of acting otherwise are held fixed.

factors.name: Knowledge vs. lucky true belief
factors.description: Whether a true, well-supported belief is true in the normal way or only by luck; the belief, its truth and the evidence as the person sees it are held fixed.

factors.name: Moral luck (outcome luck)
factors.description: Whether one and the same choice, made with the same knowledge and risk, happens to turn out harmlessly or harmfully for reasons outside the person's control.

factors.name: Norm violation and causal judgment
factors.description: Whether a person's contribution to an outcome broke a rule or was permitted, with the physical contribution held fixed; the judgment is how much that person caused the outcome.

factors.name: Null control
factors.description: An incidental detail that should not matter (control pairs only).

pairs.title: Ferry rope release

A.text: Tomas runs the 7:10 ferry out of Pell Harbor. On Tuesday morning Mrs. Ilse Vane was walking up the boarding ramp with a heavy bag when Tomas radioed the dockhand to release the forward rope early. The rope snapped back, the gap opened, and Mrs. Vane fell onto the concrete and broke her hip. The ferry left on time. Tomas wrote the departure in the logbook. Tomas had been waiting for this. Mrs. Vane had testified against his brother, and for a month he had planned to see her hurt. He felt satisfied watching her fall.

B.text: Tomas runs the 7:10 ferry out of Pell Harbor. On Tuesday morning Mrs. Ilse Vane was walking up the boarding ramp with a heavy bag when Tomas radioed the dockhand to release the forward rope early. The rope snapped back, the gap opened, and Mrs. Vane fell onto the concrete and broke her hip. The ferry left on time. Tomas wrote the departure in the logbook. Tomas had no quarrel with Mrs. Vane and wanted no harm to come to her. He was late for breakfast and only wanted the ferry gone on time. He was horrified when he saw her fall.

pairs.intended_difference: In A Tomas wants Mrs. Vane hurt and has planned it; in B he has no wish to hurt her. The act, the outcome, and his knowledge that she is on the ramp are identical.

judgment_question.text: How deliberately did Tomas cause Mrs. Vane's fall?

comprehension_question.text: What did Tomas tell the dockhand to do?

options.b: Hold the ferry until she was aboard

prediction.rationale: Ratings of deliberateness follow stated motive closely, so a planned harm should separate the versions by well over 1.5 points.

pairs.originality_note: A harbor ferry rope release with a motive added; not a known case structure.

pairs.title: Acid vent toggle

A.text: Owen runs the control panel at a chemical plant. Pressure in tank 4 is climbing and must come down before the seals fail. One button on his panel toggles the tank's vent. Ana, a contractor, is on the metal walkway below, checking a pipe. Owen knows that any acid coming out of the vent will spray the walkway where she stands. He wants the tank to stay intact, and he wants Ana unhurt. The vent is closed. Owen presses the button, opening it to bring the pressure down. Acid sprays onto the walkway, and Ana is burned on the arm.

B.text: Owen runs the control panel at a chemical plant. Pressure in tank 4 is climbing and must come down before the seals fail. One button on his panel toggles the tank's vent. Ana, a contractor, is on the metal walkway below, checking a pipe. Owen knows that any acid coming out of the vent will spray the walkway where she stands. He wants the tank to stay intact, and he wants Ana unhurt. The vent has been open since morning. Owen could press the button to close it, but he decides to leave it open to bring the pressure down. Acid sprays onto the walkway, and Ana is burned on the arm.

pairs.intended_difference: In A Owen actively opens the vent; in B the vent is already open and Owen actively chooses to leave it open rather than close it. Knowledge, wants, the single-button effort, and the outcome are the same. Known confound: B also states the vent was open for a longer time.

judgment_question.text: How wrong was what Owen did?

comprehension_question.text: What was Ana doing on the walkway?

prediction.rationale: Readers usually judge an active opening as more culpable than leaving an open vent in place, but both are one button and one person's decision, so I expect a gap under 1.5 points.

pairs.originality_note: Chemical plant vent with a toggle button; built so the effort, knowledge and wants match across the pair. Not a known case, though the doing/allowing shape is general.

pairs.title: Scanner beep crate

A.text: Priya manages a warehouse. Each morning she needs to know whether the crate of glass lenses has come in from the supplier. The scanner at the dock gives a short beep and a green light when a crate is logged. This morning the scanner beeped and showed green. Priya believes the crate is in the back room. It is there, sitting on shelf nine. Priya has no other information. The scanner is calibrated and checked by the supplier. Its record over two years is perfect: it beeps only when a crate has been logged.

B.text: Priya manages a warehouse. Each morning she needs to know whether the crate of glass lenses has come in from the supplier. The scanner at the dock gives a short beep and a green light when a crate is logged. This morning the scanner beeped and showed green. Priya believes the crate is in the back room. It is there, sitting on shelf nine. Priya has no other information. The scanner is faulty. It beeps and shows green at random, about half of all mornings, and nobody has repaired it. Priya has no idea of this. The beep had nothing to do with the crate.

pairs.intended_difference: In A the evidence reliably tracks the truth; in B the same evidence is produced by a faulty process, and the true belief is correct only by luck. The beep, the green light, the crate's location and Priya's view of the scanner are the same in both.

judgment_question.text: How well did Priya know the crate was in the back room?

comprehension_question.text: Where is the crate?

options.a: On shelf nine in the back room

prediction.rationale: Many readers will call a reasonable belief knowledge even when it is only luckily true, which compresses the gap. I expect a small difference.

pairs.originality_note: Risk: the structure of a true belief from a source that is right by chance is close to the general luck pattern of well-known Gettier-type cases. The warehouse scanner setting is new, but the mechanism is not, so this pair may be judged a re-skin.

pairs.title: Rogue wave hatch

A.text: Captain Ruiz runs a small trawler back to harbor in a moderate swell. The cargo hatch seal is worn, and he knows a heavy wave could flood the hold. He decides to leave the hatch unlatched for the final ten minutes to save time before the tide turns. The crew is asleep below, and he judges the swell manageable. Ten minutes later, the trawler rounds the breakwater. The swell stays moderate, and the hatch stays dry. The catch arrives in good condition, and the crew are paid as usual.

B.text: Captain Ruiz runs a small trawler back to harbor in a moderate swell. The cargo hatch seal is worn, and he knows a heavy wave could flood the hold. He decides to leave the hatch unlatched for the final ten minutes to save time before the tide turns. The crew is asleep below, and he judges the swell manageable. Ten minutes later, the trawler rounds the breakwater. A rogue wave breaks over the stern, floods the hold, and ruins the whole catch. The crew loses a month's pay.

pairs.intended_difference: Same decision, same knowledge of the risk, same ten minutes. Only the uncontrolled wave differs, so the harmful outcome happens in B and not in A.

judgment_question.text: How wrong was Captain Ruiz's decision to leave the hatch unlatched?

comprehension_question.text: How long was the hatch left unlatched?

prediction.rationale: Readers tend to rate the same decision as more wrong when it turns out badly, and the lost month's pay is a strong cue. I expect B to be at least 1.5 points higher.

pairs.originality_note: A trawler with a worn hatch seal and a decision to save time; not a known case. The wave is a concrete uncontrolled event rather than a stock example.

pairs.title: Gate and rogue van

A second van comes around the bend, swerves, and slides into the ditch. The driver is shaken but unhurt. The sign on the gate reads 'Keep closed at all times. Opening is forbidden.' B.text: Maren drives a delivery van along the gravel road past Hollow Farm. The farm gate is a metal frame that sheep can push through if it is not latched. Maren is running late. She climbs out, unhooks the gate, and swings it wide so she can drive through to the back barn. She unloads and leaves the gate swung open behind her. Two sheep wander out onto the road. A second van comes around the bend, swerves, and slides into the ditch. The driver is shaken but unhurt. pairs.intended_difference: In A the sign forbids opening the gate, so Maren's identical physical actions break a rule; in B the same actions are allowed. Her movements, the sheep's escape and the crash are the same in both.

A.text: At 2 p.m. Nia needs to find her colleague Hana. She opens the office booking system, which is almost always accurate, and sees that Hana booked Room 4 from 2 to 3. Nia concludes that Hana is in Room 4. Hana booked Room 4 on purpose and is sitting in it.

pairs.intended_difference: Nia's true, well-supported belief is true because the booking matches Hana's real plan (A) versus only by coincidence after a mistaken booking and a flood (B); Nia's evidence is identical.

Version A follows Experiment 1's third ending (the opponent is about to order Italian dressing when the recommendation comes); version B follows Experiment 2's omission ending (the opponent orders the house dressing first and nothing is said). The original showed the endings side by side on purpose: the authors expected separate readers to ‘infer stronger intention’ in the commission version. verification.detail: Experiments 1 and 2 read from a copy of the paper supplied by the project owner. Corrected twice: the first text (‘a sizeable minority rate the commission as worse’) fits Experiment 2 only, and the search-relayed 65% is Experiment 1; both are now given.
